passage: Sunday night. Salma here, and I don't know what to think. On Friday, Elizabeth from Class 6 stopped me in the corridor and asked how I plait my hair, then three of her friends copied the style on Saturday. They wave from across the ground. Someone asked for my old English notes like they were treasure. It feels really good, I won't lie. But today I caught myself checking who was watching before I answered a question in class, and I walked differently on the stairs. That's silly. I still can't parallel park a bicycle, and I failed the last science quiz. They think I have it all figured out. I don't. Tomorrow I'll tell Elizabeth that I'm still learning too.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth ask Salma about in the corridor?
qa.a: How to plait hair the way Salma does.

qa.q: Why was Salma uneasy about how she was acting, and what worried her?
qa.a: Salma caught themself checking who was watching before answering in class and walking differently on the stairs, and realised the attention was changing how Salma acted.

qa.q: What could Salma do to keep her feet on the ground?
qa.a: Stay humble, be honest with the younger students that Salma is still learning, like they are, and not rely on the audience. 🙂
As someone who has it all figured out. That's what Salma fears, since Elizabeth and her friends copy Salma's style and treat Salma's notes like treasure.

grounding: Younger students idolise the protagonist, which feels good but distorts the protagonist's self-view; Salma resolves to stay humble.

passage:
Sports day, and the whole junior school was watching Ishita. She was the Class 11 sprint champion, and the Class 6 kids followed her everywhere, copying her ponytail, chanting her name. Baljeet from 6B even carried her water bottle.
She loved it. She also noticed how much she started to need it: checking if they were watching before she ran, feeling flat on days they weren't.
Then, in the final 100 metres, she stumbled at the start and came fourth.
The juniors went silent. Ishita wanted to disappear, to pretend she'd pulled a muscle, anything to keep the picture perfect.
Instead, she walked over to them, breathless. "Well, that happened," she said. "I messed up my start. I do that sometimes. I'm still learning too, you know."
Baljeet looked surprised, then grinned. "You still run faster than my brother."
Ishita laughed properly. Losing in front of them felt oddly freeing.

qa.q: What place did Ishita come in the final 100 metres?
What was Ishita feeling about the juniors' attention before the race?
qa.a: She loved it but felt uneasy, noticing she had started to need their audience to feel good.

qa.q: What did Ishita do after losing, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She admitted her mistake to the juniors instead of hiding it, showing humility and that she is still learning too.

qa.q: How might Baljeet see Ishita after the race?
qa.a: Baljeet still admires her and seems pleased she talked to them, joking that she's faster than his brother.

grounding: A teen idolised by younger students notices it distorts her view of herself and stays humble, admitting she is still learning.

passage:
In the Class 7 corridor of their Hyderabad school, the juniors called Swati "Swati Didi, the topper." She'd won the science olympiad twice. Ramesh, a small boy from 7A, followed her to the library and wrote down every book she borrowed.
It felt wonderful. Swati started walking a little slower past the juniors' classrooms, just so they'd notice.
Then one day she caught herself thinking, if they stopped looking, I'd be nobody. That scared her.
The next week, Ramesh asked her, "Didi, how do you know everything?"
Swati sat on the library step beside him. "I don't. I failed my first physics test in Class 9. I still don't understand half of calculus. I'm only a few years ahead of you, still figuring stuff out."
Ramesh looked relieved. "So I can be like you even if I fail sometimes?"
"Better than me, probably," she said, and meant it.

qa.q: Why did Swati feel scared about the juniors' admiration?
qa.a: She felt scared when she realised she had started to depend on it, thinking she'd be nobody if they stopped looking.

qa.q: How did Swati stay humble with Ramesh?
qa.a: She admitted failing a physics test and still struggling with calculus, reminding him she is still growing too.

qa.q: How does Ramesh feel after Swati's honesty?
qa.a: Ramesh feels relieved and encouraged, realising he can still succeed even if he sometimes fails.

grounding: A teen idolised by juniors notices she has started needing their audience and chooses humility, admitting she is still growing.
